lines.text: In 1919, a wave of molasses killed twenty-one people.
This tank, five stories tall, held two point three million gallons of molasses.
And it leaked from day one.
The man in charge had no engineering experience, and skipped a proper water test.
When the leaks got worse, he had the tank painted brown to hide them.
Then, after a bitter cold snap, the temperature shot past forty degrees.
Around twelve forty, rivets burst out like machine-gun fire.
A wave up to twenty-five feet high raced through the streets at thirty-five miles an hour,
knocking buildings off their foundations and slamming into the elevated railway.
But speed wasn't the deadliest part.
As the air froze that night, the molasses thickened. Scientists estimate at least four times.
About half the victims died simply because they were stuck.
For decades, locals said the North End smelled sweet on hot days.
